acc-b1-summarize-financial-document-safe.q: A colleague wants to summarize a client's unredacted trial balance using a public AI chatbot to save time before a meeting. What should you tell them?
options: Strip or replace client names, account numbers, and other identifying details with placeholders before pasting anything
Go ahead, as long as the summary is checked for accuracy afterward
It's fine since the AI tool's chat history is private to their account
Only remove the client name, since account numbers aren't sensitive
acc-b1-summarize-financial-document-safe.why: Pasting an unredacted client file into a general-purpose AI tool creates a confidentiality risk regardless of accuracy checks afterward; identifying details must be stripped or replaced with placeholders first.

acc-b1-summarize-financial-document-safe.q: Why does the summarization prompt explicitly instruct the AI to say "not stated in the document" instead of guessing when something is unclear?
options: It makes the summary shorter and faster to generate
It prevents the AI from filling gaps with plausible-sounding but invented figures that could end up in client advice
It is required by most AI tools' terms of service
It allows the AI to skip sections it finds difficult
acc-b1-summarize-financial-document-safe.why: The biggest risk with AI summaries of financial material is confident-sounding but wrong numbers; explicitly flagging uncertainty stops the AI from inventing details to fill gaps.

acc-b1-summarize-financial-document-safe.q: After generating a structured summary of a 40-page lease accounting standard, what is the required next step before using any figure from it in client advice?
options: Send it to the client immediately since the AI was told to only use stated facts
Ask the AI a second time to confirm its own summary is accurate
Independently verify every number, date, and figure in the summary against the source document
Round all figures for simplicity before sharing them
acc-b1-summarize-financial-document-safe.why: Even with grounding instructions, every number, date, and figure must be independently verified against the original document before it's used in any client communication.

acc-b2-notes-to-client-explanation.q: You paste rough session notes into the prompt to generate a client-facing explanation. What is the most important check before sending the draft?
options: Checking that the AI used a friendly tone throughout
Making sure the explanation is at least five paragraphs long
Verifying the AI defined every accounting term twice
Confirming every number and fact matches your original notes exactly, with no rounding or restating
acc-b2-notes-to-client-explanation.why: The most common failure mode is the AI 'helpfully' rounding or restating a figure; every number must be confirmed to match the original notes exactly before the draft is used.

acc-b2-notes-to-client-explanation.q: Why does the prompt ask you to name the specific audience (e.g. "a small business owner with no accounting background") rather than just saying "write for a client"?
options: Because naming the exact audience is what makes the explanation genuinely readable instead of generic
Because the AI cannot generate output without an audience specified
Because it changes the required length of the response
Because it determines which AI model should be used
acc-b2-notes-to-client-explanation.why: Naming the specific audience and their financial literacy level is what makes the resulting explanation land as genuinely readable rather than a generic, textbook-style answer.

acc-b2-notes-to-client-explanation.q: What is the correct way to handle the client's real name when using this prompt in a shared or logged AI account?
options: Use the real name so the draft feels more personal
Replace it with a placeholder like [CLIENT] in the notes you paste, and add the real name back only after moving the text out of the AI tool
Use only the client's first name as a compromise
Ask the AI to redact the name automatically after generating the draft
acc-b2-notes-to-client-explanation.why: The client's real name should stay out of the AI tool entirely; a placeholder is used during generation and the real name is added back only after the text has left the AI tool.

acc-b3-client-reminders-and-requests.q: A client has ignored two prior reminders for missing bank statements. What should change in your next AI-drafted reminder compared to the first one you sent?
options: Nothing, the same friendly tone should always be used to preserve the relationship
The email should double in length to show seriousness
The tone should shift to firm, since the prompt is designed to support both a first friendly reminder and a firmer follow-up
The deadline should be removed since it clearly isn't working
acc-b3-client-reminders-and-requests.why: The prompt is explicitly parameterized for tone (friendly first reminder vs. firm follow-up), and using the same friendly tone indefinitely after being ignored is a listed common mistake.

acc-b3-client-reminders-and-requests.q: Why does the prompt instruct the AI not to state any penalty amount or legal consequence you haven't specified?
options: Because penalties are never relevant to accounting deadlines
Because mentioning penalties is against most email service providers' policies
Because it shortens the email automatically
Because it prevents the AI from adding a plausible-sounding but inaccurate consequence for that specific client's situation
acc-b3-client-reminders-and-requests.why: Letting the AI invent a penalty or legal consequence you didn't specify risks stating something inaccurate for that client's actual situation, which the guardrail is designed to prevent.

acc-b3-client-reminders-and-requests.q: What is the single biggest driver of client response rate according to this lesson, and how should it be handled in the prompt?
options: A concrete, clearly stated deadline included in the prompt inputs
A long, detailed explanation of accounting terminology
Using bold and colorful formatting in the email
CC'ing the client's business partner on every reminder
acc-b3-client-reminders-and-requests.why: The lesson identifies a concrete stated deadline as the single biggest driver of client response rate, and forgetting to include one is listed as a common mistake.

acc-b4-explain-financial-concepts-plain-.q: A client asks why they owe tax on money they haven't received yet. Why does the prompt explicitly forbid the AI from stating specific tax rates or thresholds?
options: Tax rates are considered trade secrets
Rates and thresholds vary by jurisdiction and change over time, so an AI stating one with confidence is a common source of bad advice if unchecked
The AI is incapable of producing numbers accurately
Clients generally don't care about specific numbers
acc-b4-explain-financial-concepts-plain-.why: Specific tax rates and thresholds depend on jurisdiction and change over time, so banning them from the AI's output is a guardrail against a common source of bad advice.

acc-b4-explain-financial-concepts-plain-.q: What makes the analogy in a generated explanation actually effective for the client, according to this lesson?
options: Using the most technically precise analogy available, regardless of the client's business
Using multiple analogies to cover all possible interpretations
Grounding the request in the client's actual business context so the analogy is relevant rather than generic
Letting the AI choose any well-known analogy from finance textbooks
acc-b4-explain-financial-concepts-plain-.why: Grounding the explanation in the client's actual business (e.g. a cafe with same-day sales but some supplier credit) is what makes the analogy land instead of feeling like a generic textbook definition.

acc-b4-explain-financial-concepts-plain-.q: Before sending an AI-generated plain-language explanation of a financial concept to a client, what must the accountant do?
options: Nothing further, since the prompt already bans invented rates
Ask a second AI tool to double-check the first one's output
Only check that the word count is under the limit
Personally confirm the explanation is technically accurate for that client's specific situation and jurisdiction
acc-b4-explain-financial-concepts-plain-.why: The accountant must always verify the explanation is technically accurate for the specific client's situation and jurisdiction before sending, since an oversimplified explanation can become technically incorrect and create liability.

acc-b5-internal-checklists-and-process-d.q: The AI suggests an additional step for a month-end close checklist that you never actually described. Where should this suggestion appear in the output?
options: In a separate "possible gaps to review" section, not inside the main checklist
Merged directly into the numbered checklist since the AI is usually right
It should be silently deleted from the response
Sent to the whole team as an urgent update
acc-b5-internal-checklists-and-process-d.why: The prompt requires AI-suggested additions to be listed separately under 'possible gaps to review' rather than folded into the official checklist, preventing an invented step from silently becoming part of the real process.

acc-b5-internal-checklists-and-process-d.q: Why does the prompt ask for a "common failure points" section listing steps like cutoff errors or unreconciled accounts?
options: Because every checklist must legally include a risk disclaimer
Because it draws on general accounting risk patterns to highlight where mistakes are most likely, without pretending to know the firm's specific practice
Because it replaces the need for a technical accuracy review
Because it makes the checklist longer and more thorough-looking
acc-b5-internal-checklists-and-process-d.why: The common-failure-points section draws on general accounting risk patterns like cutoff timing and unreconciled control accounts, adding real value without claiming firm-specific knowledge.

acc-b5-internal-checklists-and-process-d.q: A junior staff member publishes the first AI-generated checklist draft to the team without changes. What mistake did they make?
options: They should have asked the AI to make the checklist longer first
They should have used a different AI tool
They skipped reviewing the checklist against actual practice before publishing it to the team
There was no mistake, since the AI already flagged uncertain steps
acc-b5-internal-checklists-and-process-d.why: The workflow requires reviewing the checklist against actual practice and correcting it before it becomes official; skipping this step and publishing the first draft directly is a listed common mistake.

acc-i1-analyze-variance-narrative.q: Why must variance amounts and percentages be calculated in your accounting system or spreadsheet before being given to the AI, rather than letting the AI calculate them?
options: AI tools cannot process numeric data at all
It makes the prompt shorter
Accounting software is always faster than AI at calculations
Large language models can make arithmetic mistakes, so keeping number-crunching outside the AI removes the risk of a silent error in a management report
acc-i1-analyze-variance-narrative.why: The explicit instruction that all figures are already calculated and must not be recalculated is the most important guardrail, since a single AI arithmetic error inserted into a management report can be costly.

acc-i1-analyze-variance-narrative.q: A material variance has no explanatory note attached to it. What should the AI do with that line item?
options: List it under "needs explanation from me" rather than inventing a reason
Invent the most statistically likely explanation based on general accounting patterns
Omit the variance from the report entirely
Mark it as immaterial regardless of its size
acc-i1-analyze-variance-narrative.why: Unexplained material variances must be routed to a 'needs explanation from me' list rather than filled in with a guessed reason, preventing fabricated explanations from reaching a management report.

acc-i1-analyze-variance-narrative.q: Who should set the materiality threshold used to separate variances that need a written explanation from those that don't?
options: The AI, based on general best practices it has learned
The accountant or firm/client, using a threshold they control and specify in the prompt
Whichever threshold produces the shortest narrative
It doesn't matter as long as a threshold exists
acc-i1-analyze-variance-narrative.why: Using a materiality threshold the AI invented instead of one the firm or client actually uses is listed as a common mistake; the threshold should be supplied by the accountant.

acc-i2-meeting-agendas-followup-summarie.q: Your raw meeting notes don't specify who owns a particular action item. How should the follow-up summary prompt handle this?
options: The AI should assign the most likely owner based on typical meeting patterns
The action item should be dropped from the summary entirely
Use "TBD" for the missing owner or due date rather than inventing one
The accountant should always be assumed as the default owner
acc-i2-meeting-agendas-followup-summarie.why: The prompt specifies a 'TBD' fallback for missing owners or dates, stopping the AI from silently assigning an action item or deadline that was never actually agreed on.

acc-i2-meeting-agendas-followup-summarie.q: Why does the follow-up summary structure keep "decisions made" separate from general discussion points and open questions?
options: To make the document longer and more formal-looking
Because clients prefer longer documents
It is a legal requirement for meeting minutes
Because mixing general discussion with firm decisions makes it unclear what was actually agreed
acc-i2-meeting-agendas-followup-summarie.why: Mixing general discussion points in with firm decisions is a listed common mistake because it makes it unclear what was actually agreed versus merely discussed.

acc-i2-meeting-agendas-followup-summarie.q: Before sending the post-meeting follow-up summary to the client, what should you do?
options: Verify every number and decision in the summary against your raw notes
Send it immediately since the AI was instructed to use only the notes provided
Ask the client to verify it themselves
Shorten it further to under 50 words
acc-i2-meeting-agendas-followup-summarie.why: The workflow requires verifying every number and decision in the summary against your raw notes before sending it to the client, since even grounded summaries can misstate details.

acc-i3-reusable-prompt-templates-client-.q: Why does this lesson start from your own best real example of a message type, instead of asking the AI to write a generic template from scratch?
options: Generic templates take longer for the AI to generate
Starting from your real example keeps the resulting template in your actual voice and matching how your firm really communicates
AI tools require a source example to function
It reduces the number of placeholders needed
acc-i3-reusable-prompt-templates-client-.why: Building the template from your own tested example, rather than generic AI writing, is what keeps the output authentic to your firm's actual communication style.

acc-i3-reusable-prompt-templates-client-.q: The prompt asks the AI to flag which placeholders are "especially risky" if left wrong or outdated. What kind of placeholder does this typically refer to?
options: The greeting and sign-off lines
The subject line of the email
Specific dollar amounts and deadlines, since using a stale or wrong figure there is most likely to cause harm
General tone descriptors like "warm" or "professional"
acc-i3-reusable-prompt-templates-client-.why: The risk-flagging step draws attention to placeholders like dollar amounts and deadlines, which are the most likely to cause real harm if left stale or incorrect.

acc-i3-reusable-prompt-templates-client-.q: A template uses a vague placeholder like [DETAILS] instead of [REVENUE FIGURE] or [DUE DATE]. What problem does this create?
options: No real problem, since the AI can infer the right value each time
It only affects formatting, not content
It makes the template load slower
It increases the risk of accidentally leaving irrelevant or outdated information in the message since it's not obvious what must change each time
acc-i3-reusable-prompt-templates-client-.why: Vague placeholders instead of specific, clearly bracketed ones is a listed common mistake, since specific placeholders make it obvious at a glance what must be updated each use.

acc-i4-structure-data-cleaning-instructi.q: You need help writing a data-cleaning procedure for a messy bank export. What should you paste into the AI prompt?
options: A description of the columns and problems, plus a few fake sample rows with the same pattern as the real data
The full real client export so the AI can see the actual problems
Only the column headers, with no sample data at all
A screenshot of the real spreadsheet
acc-i4-structure-data-cleaning-instructi.why: The cleaning logic depends only on the pattern of the mess, not the actual transactions, so a description plus fake sample rows avoids exposing real client data while still producing a usable procedure.

acc-i4-structure-data-cleaning-instructi.q: Why does the prompt ask for a verification check after each major cleaning step, rather than just one check at the very end?
options: It makes the output longer, which looks more thorough
It turns the cleanup into something auditable, with checkpoints a reviewer can retrace later
Spreadsheet software requires a check after every formula
It reduces the number of formulas needed
acc-i4-structure-data-cleaning-instructi.why: A verification check after each major step creates a documented, auditable procedure with checkpoints, rather than an untraceable series of manual edits if a reviewer later asks how the data was prepared.

acc-i4-structure-data-cleaning-instructi.q: After running a generated cleaning procedure on the real spreadsheet, what is the most important final check?
options: Confirming the spreadsheet file size decreased
Checking that all formulas use the same color formatting
Comparing the original row count and control total to the cleaned row count and total to catch silent data loss
Verifying the AI's response was under a certain word count
acc-i4-structure-data-cleaning-instructi.why: The final reconciliation check, comparing row count and control total before and after cleaning, is the single most important check for catching silently dropped or duplicated rows.

acc-i5-procedure-docs-and-staff-training.q: Why does this lesson insist on including the reasoning behind key decisions, not just the mechanical steps, when generating training documentation?
options: It makes the document meet a required minimum length
Reasoning is only needed for compliance audits
It reduces the number of practice questions needed
New hires who understand why a step exists make better judgment calls when they hit an edge case the document didn't anticipate
acc-i5-procedure-docs-and-staff-training.why: Training material built on reasoning, not just mechanical steps, helps trainees adapt when they encounter situations the document didn't explicitly cover.

acc-i5-procedure-docs-and-staff-training.q: The AI suggests the documentation is missing a step about escalating unresolved discrepancies, something the original expert never mentioned. Where should this go?
options: Into a separate "gaps to confirm with the author" section, kept apart from the authoritative content
Inserted directly into the numbered steps since it sounds reasonable
Deleted from the response entirely
Added as a footnote without review
acc-i5-procedure-docs-and-staff-training.why: AI-suggested additions are isolated into a 'gaps to confirm with the author' section so the authoritative document stays limited to what the actual expert verified.

acc-i5-procedure-docs-and-staff-training.q: What is the most reliable way to catch gaps in a finished training document, according to this lesson's pro tip?
options: Having the original author re-read their own document
Having a recently onboarded team member follow the document exactly as written and flag anywhere they got stuck
Running the document through a grammar checker
Asking the AI to grade its own output
acc-i5-procedure-docs-and-staff-training.why: The lesson notes that having a recently onboarded team member follow the document as written catches gaps far more reliably than the original author reviewing their own work.
